<reason>A wins by more clearly isolating pricing’s incremental benefits and burdens. Registration, enforcement, reservations, and time-varying loading rules answer much of B’s contrast between prices and unmanaged queues. B retains a credible marginal-incentive argument, strengthened by the motion’s permissive wording, but never adequately weighs that benefit against charging inflexible users or excluding necessary trips by ability to pay. Its claims that only prices reveal scarcity or enable responsive management are directly rebutted. A’s comparative case is stronger, though pricing’s plausible behavioral benefits keep the result competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A decisively challenged B’s “tie in the worst case and a win everywhere else”: unchanged demand leaves scarcity plus a charge, while reduced demand does not establish that flexible discretionary users leave rather than low-margin necessary users. This exposed the missing distributional weighing in B’s final argument.</best_rebuttal>
